meaning: A slice of ownership in a company.
A list of companies whose combined price tracks a market, like the FTSE 100.
A pot of many investors' money, spread across many holdings by a manager.
A fund that trades on a stock exchange like a share. Most track an index.
A company listed in London whose business is owning other investments, such as wind farms.
Cash a company pays to shareholders out of its profits.
How London quotes most prices. 2,485p is £24.85.
Share price times number of shares: what the market says the whole company is worth.
A UK account where investment gains and dividends are tax-free, up to £20,000 paid in per tax year.
Ongoing charges figure: a fund's yearly fee, taken from inside the fund.
A 0.5% UK tax when you buy most UK shares. ETFs are exempt.
What a platform charges to convert pounds into dollars or euros to buy a foreign share.
The gap between the price you can buy at and the price you can sell at.
Part of one share, so £300 can buy into a £1,200 share.
How much and how fast a price swings.
A yardstick, usually an index fund, to judge your results against.
One hundredth of a percentage point. A yield rising 25bp goes from 4.00% to 4.25%.
The interest rate a government or company pays to borrow, as a % per year.
A company's report of sales and profits for a quarter or half-year.
Initial public offering: a company selling shares to the public for the first time.
Environmental, social and governance: rules used to screen out or favour companies.
The bid is the best price a buyer will pay right now; the ask (or offer) is the lowest price a seller will accept.
The live list of buy and sell orders for a share, showing how many shares people want to trade at each price.
A firm that is always ready to buy and sell a share, earning the spread in return.
Buying and selling that happens after the main exchange session closes, often when companies release results.
The US inflation measure the Federal Reserve watches most closely, based on what people actually spend money on.
Building an index so bigger companies (by total market value) count for more of its moves than smaller ones.
A bond issued by the UK government; its yield is the interest rate the government pays to borrow.
Capital expenditure: money a company spends on long-lasting things like data centres, factories or equipment.
The cash a business has left after paying its running costs and its capex.
How many shares are rising versus falling, which shows whether a market move is broad or driven by a few big names.
The Bank of England's main interest rate, which influences mortgage, savings and borrowing rates across the UK.
A fund that simply copies an index, such as the FTSE 100, instead of having a manager pick shares; it is usually cheap.
The value of everything a fund or investment trust owns, minus its debts, usually given per share.
When an investment trust's share price is below its NAV; the opposite, a price above NAV, is a premium.
When a company uses spare cash to buy back its own shares, leaving each remaining share a bigger slice of the company.
The forecast a company gives for its own future sales or profits.
Gross domestic product: the total value of everything an economy produces, the main measure of growth.
Spreading your money across many different investments so that one bad result can't do too much damage.
How closely two investments move together; highly correlated shares tend to rise and fall at the same time.
An index of how much turbulence investors expect in US shares over the next month, often called the 'fear gauge'.
A computer chip, or the industry that designs, makes and supplies the machines for making chips.
How far an investment has fallen from its previous peak, in per cent, before it recovers.
American depositary receipt: a certificate traded in New York that stands for shares in a foreign company, such as Novo Nordisk.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, deciding control of Congress (the House and Senate).
How much ups and downs in value you can live with, both in money and in nerves, without selling at the wrong time.
